And Rabsaces said to them: Say to Hezekiah: Thus says the great king of Assyria: Is it by counsel or words of lips that a battle array is formed? Now, on whom do you trust, that you rebel against me? Behold, you trust in the staff of Egypt, which is a broken reed, and whoever leans on it will pierce his hand. This is Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and all who trust in him. When the gates are shut and the walls are manned by the most valiant people, the need for ambassadors is fulfilled, and the chosen ones of the king go out to Rabsaces, and they make offerings. But Rabsaces, being of Persian harshness and having a mouth that speaks great things, according to what is written, blasphemes against the glory of God. And he calls Hezekiah by name only, without adding 'king'. He says that the king of Assyria is not simply called so, but also great. And he says, 'Is it by counsel or words of lips that a battle array is formed?' Because the Jews, having the law through Moses, thought themselves wiser than other nations; and indeed they said, 'We are blessed, Israel, because we know what is pleasing to the Lord.' But Rabsaces brings down their boast of war and battle, saying that it will be completely useless for them to have knowledge of laws, and to be wise in counsel, and to have only words.

Since some of the Judean rulers have called upon the Egyptians for help, and are doing this in vain, the Assyrian now thinks that Hezekiah does not trust in God, but in others, namely those who possess the land of the Egyptians. For the hope in them is fragile and always easily broken, and it wrongs rather than benefits those who use it. Like a reed, which if someone leans on it, will surely break and wrong the one who trusts in it. But if you say: 'We trust in the Lord our God,' now make a deal with my lord the king of Assyria, and I will give you two thousand horses, if you can provide riders for them. And how can you resist the face of one of the governors? He is again speaking blasphemy, and his horn is lifted up, and he speaks injustice against God. For if you have trusted in Him, make a deal with my lord, that is, arm yourselves and stand for battle. And I will add, and give you two thousand horses, and this will be enough.
pass_b_english: Rabsaces, the messenger of the king of Assyria, addressed Hezekiah with a message from his master, saying that the great king of Assyria wished to know on whom Hezekiah relied for support, since he had rebelled against him.

Rabsaces pointed out that Egypt, on whom Hezekiah seemed to be relying, was a broken reed that would pierce the hand of anyone who leaned on it, as he said, 'Behold, you trust in the staff of Egypt, which is a broken reed, and whoever leans on it will pierce his hand' (Isaiah 36:6).

The king of Egypt, Pharaoh, was not a reliable ally, and those who trusted in him would be disappointed, for Rabsaces called him a broken reed, saying that all who trust in him will be wronged, rather than benefited.

When a city was besieged and its walls were manned by brave warriors, the need for ambassadors was clear, and the chosen representatives of the king would go out to negotiate with Rabsaces, who was known for his harsh and boastful speech.

Rabsaces blasphemed against the glory of God, saying 'Is it by counsel or words of lips that a battle array is formed?' (Isaiah 36:4), implying that the Jews' trust in their wisdom and knowledge of the law would not save them from the Assyrian army.

The Jews thought themselves wise and blessed because they had the law of Moses, and indeed they said, 'We are blessed, Israel, because we know what is pleasing to the Lord' (Isaiah 36:10), but Rabsaces argued that this would be of no use to them in the face of the enemy.

Rabsaces believed that Hezekiah did not trust in God, but rather in the Egyptians who possess the land, and that this hope was fragile and easily broken, much like a reed that will surely break if someone leans on it, and will wrong the one who trusts in it.

The commander's words were laced with blasphemy, as he lifted up his horn and spoke injustice against God, challenging the Judeans to make a deal with his lord, the king of Assyria, if they truly trusted in the Lord their God.

He said, 'if you say: We trust in the Lord our God, now make a deal with my lord the king of Assyria, and I will give you two thousand horses, if you can provide riders for them' (Isaiah 36:8), and 'how can you resist the face of just one of the Assyrian governors?'

Furthermore, Rabsaces said, 'if you have trusted in Him, make a deal with my lord, that is, arm yourselves and stand for battle, and I will add, and give you two thousand horses, and this will be enough' (Isaiah 36:9).
Rabsaces also called Hezekiah by name only, without adding 'king', which was a title most becoming for a ruler, and he referred to the king of Assyria as not simply a king, but a great king.

The Jews, having the law through Moses, thought themselves wiser than other nations, but Rabsaces brought down their boast of war and battle, saying that it will be completely useless for them to have knowledge of laws, and to be wise in counsel, and to have only words.
